name: Video-metadata micro-artifact review lead for live deepfake interviews

attribution.legal_posture: Cloudforce One's published assessment is retained as an evidence-limited review lead; validation methods and detector performance remain unpublished by the source.

caveats: Apply this signal within human review and corroboration, rather than as an automated rejection rule.
Faceprints, raw interview video, and biometric templates are excluded from this dataset.
A metadata anomaly calls for review; deepfake use, fraudulent employment, nationality, and DPRK affiliation require corroboration.

Retain the video-metadata item only as a vendor-assessed corroborating lead. Candidate rejection and DPRK attribution require separate evidence. The report's biometrics-only recommendation requires privacy, accessibility, legal, spoof-resistance, and non-biometric-alternative safeguards before defensive use.
The report omits technical definition, implementation detail, test corpus, sample size, sensitivity, specificity, and false-positive rate.

statements: Cloudforce One identifies specific video metadata micro-artifacts consistent with real-time deepfake rendering as one of several high-fidelity indicators in North Korean remote IT-worker schemes.
The vendor’s metadata-layer micro-artifact concept is a proposed corroborating lead, not a validated detection method.

Materially new but evidence-limited lead: preserve conferencing metadata only when lawful and necessary for security review, assess source-described metadata-layer rendering anomalies, and require independent identity, device, location, and hiring-process evidence before escalation.
limitations: The report provides no technical definition, implementation detail, test corpus, sample size, sensitivity, specificity, or false-positive rate.
Video metadata can be altered by legitimate conferencing software, accessibility tooling, virtual backgrounds, bandwidth adaptation, recording, privacy tools, and ordinary media processing.

The source's recommendation for zero-trust biometric verification is not adopted here; any identity-assurance control requires privacy, accessibility, legal, retention, consent, spoof-resistance, and non-biometric-alternative review.
Do not treat a metadata anomaly as proof of deepfake use, fraudulent employment, nationality, or DPRK affiliation.
Do not retain faceprints, raw interview video, or biometric templates in this dataset.
Do not apply this signal as an automated rejection rule.

Retain the video-metadata item only as a vendor-assessed corroborating lead. Do not use it alone to reject a candidate or attribute DPRK affiliation. Do not adopt the report's biometrics-only recommendation as a defensive control without privacy, accessibility, legal, spoof-resistance, and non-biometric-alternative safeguards.

sources.support: Cloudforce One describes North Korean remote IT-worker schemes as an industrialized insider threat using fraudulent identities, AI-driven deepfakes, U.S.-based laptop farms, facilitators, RMM access, and comprehensive LinkedIn and GitHub personas. Alongside impossible-travel and mouse-jiggling indicators, Cloudforce One identifies video metadata micro-artifacts consistent with real-time deepfake rendering as a high-fidelity detection indicator. The source reports publication timing only at year precision: 2026; published_at is therefore left null rather than inventing a day. The PDF metadata records document creation on 2026-03-23; this is not asserted as the public release date.
